Yes — validation evidence, once produced, remains adequate indefinitely
Only the vendor can determine if evidence needs refreshing

hints: The generalization problem from lesson 2 applies across time within the same health system, not just across different health systems.
A significant new population (a new specialty) is functionally similar to deploying to a new environment.
explanation: The same generalization concern that makes a vendor's cross-system study insufficient applies within one health system over time — an evidence base from 18 months ago doesn't automatically cover a materially different population added since, and a fresh, targeted local check is warranted.

prompt: A vendor ships a "major" version update that, per their own description, only changes the UI layout of the coder review screen with no change to underlying model behavior. What tier does this warrant?

options.text: No additional review, if genuinely confirmed to have no functional/behavioral change — the 'major' label alone doesn't override that
Full re-validation automatically, because it's labeled 'major'
It's impossible to tell without more information than given

hints: This is the mirror image of the earlier 'minor label, real behavioral change' example — apply the same functional-risk test in the other direction.
The vendor's label was identified as unreliable in both directions, not just as a source of false reassurance.
explanation: This is the deliberate mirror case: just as a "minor" label can hide a real behavioral change, a "major" label can describe a change with zero functional risk (pure UI). The tier should be set by the functional-risk questions, not the vendor's label, in either direction.

statement: An incident that a patient or family never complains about cannot carry an external reporting obligation.

config.statement: An incident that a patient or family never complains about cannot carry an external reporting obligation.
config.rubric: Full credit notes reporting obligations are generally tied to the nature/severity of the event and function involved, independent of whether a complaint was ever filed.

hints: Where does a reporting obligation actually come from, per this module?
Relying on the absence of a complaint as a filter was explicitly flagged as a governance risk in lesson 4.
explanation: False. Reporting obligations, where they exist, are generally tied to the severity and function of what happened, not to whether anyone outside the organization became aware and complained — treating 'no complaint' as evidence that nothing needs reporting is exactly the governance risk this module warns against.

prompt: A new pipeline proposal includes a validation plan but no chain-mapping analysis of what could go wrong and where it would be caught. By this module's pre-go-live standard, is the proposal ready for go-live review?

options.text: No — chain mapping is one of the five required checklist categories; missing it is a real gap, not a minor omission
Yes — validation evidence alone is sufficient for go-live readiness
It depends only on how confident the engineering team feels

hints: Recall the five checklist categories from lesson 5 — validation is only one of them.
A 'no' or 'unclear' on any checklist item was explicitly called a real blocker, not a note for later.
explanation: The pre-go-live checklist has five distinct categories, and chain mapping is one of them — a proposal with strong validation evidence but no chain analysis is still missing a required category, and per lesson 5, a missing or unclear item on any of the five is a real blocker, not something to defer.

prompt: Sort each pre-go-live checklist item by which of the five categories from lesson 5 it belongs to.

items.text: Does this feature act with human review before clinical effect, or more autonomously?
Do we have our own population's performance data, not just the vendor's?
Is there an agreed process for classifying future updates by functional risk?
Is there a standing process for flagging Critical-severity, regulated-function incidents to compliance?
Has someone traced what this pipeline could get wrong and which systems would inherit that error?

hints: Each item maps directly to one of this module's five lessons.
This is a direct recall of the checklist structure from lesson 5.
explanation: Each checklist item corresponds to exactly one of the five lesson frameworks this module built: functional classification, local validation evidence, update-risk tiering, incident routing, and chain mapping — together they form the complete pre-go-live standard.

prompt: A colleague argues that pre-go-live governance checklists like this module's slow down deployment without adding real safety value. Write a two-to-three sentence response grounded in this phase's cost logic (not just "safety matters").
hints: Compare the cost of answering a checklist question now versus reconstructing the same answer after an incident.
This phase has made a specific, repeated argument about the relative cost of proactive versus reactive work — use it.
explanation: A strong answer makes the cost argument explicitly, not just an appeal to safety in the abstract: every question on this checklist is one this phase has shown gets asked anyway, eventually, during an audit or after an incident — the only choice is whether it gets answered now, as a checklist item, or later, under worse conditions, after a patient has already been affected. The checklist doesn't add a new cost; it moves an existing one to the cheapest possible point to pay it.
